implementation_notes: Guava's Striped is the reusable form of the pattern the catalog cites: Striped.lock(n) or Striped.lazyWeakLock(n) returns an object whose get(key) always yields the same lock for equal keys, with collisions possible but harmless; striped.get(key).lock() ... unlock() brackets the critical section, and bulkGet(keys) returns the needed stripes in ascending index order so multi-key operations cannot deadlock. Striped.readWriteLock(n) provides the reader-writer flavor. Choose the weak factory when many stripes are created but only a few are used.
pitfalls: Two different keys may map to the same lock: code that locks keys a and b in one critical section must use bulkGet (which returns stripes in ascending order and may repeat one) instead of locking the two keys in ad-hoc order.
Guava's weak stripes can be reclaimed when nobody references them; holding Lock references for long periods defeats weak semantics and pins the memory the weak factory was meant to free.
get() requires a well-behaved equals/hashCode; mutable or incorrectly hashed keys break the guarantee that equal keys share a stripe.

variants.name: Hand-rolled ReentrantLock stripes
variants.implementation_notes: Without Guava, allocate a ReentrantLock[] of n stripes and select one with Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), n) (floorMod, not %, so negative hashes stay in range). The array is created eagerly; lazy or reclaimable stripes can be emulated with a ConcurrentHashMap<Integer, Lock> plus computeIfAbsent, at the price of a map lookup on every access. Multi-key operations lock the distinct stripe indices in ascending order and release them in reverse.
pitfalls: key.hashCode() may be negative and changes for mutable keys; floorMod keeps the index in range but does not repair an unstable hash.
ReentrantLock hides re-acquisition of the same stripe from a nested call, which can mask an ordering bug until two different stripes are involved and the program deadlocks.
